note: The declared skips. Every entry names a test that is allowed to skip and says why.
A skip is a suite whose assertions did not run, so the default answer is that it is a
failure. `internal/skipaudit` reads this file and fails the gate on anything not declared
here. The list is printed on every verification run whether or not its entries fired, because
an exemption list nobody re-reads is one that gets widened without anybody noticing.
The rules this file has to keep:
- one test per entry, named `package.Test`, never a package
- `why` is mandatory and the gate refuses a blank one
- `when`, when present, names the GOOS values the declaration applies to. A skip gated on a
platform is conditional in BOTH directions: on the other platform the test runs, so an
unscoped declaration would be reported as stale there, and a gate that can only be
satisfied on one platform is a gate that gets disabled on the other
- a declaration for a test that no longer skips on its platform FAILS the gate, so a removed
test cannot leave behind an exemption for whatever gets named next
- a missing file is a refusal, not an empty allow-list
These five were read off a real run rather than guessed. Each entry below is a skip this
repository already makes deliberately, in every run, on this machine.

declared.why: creating a symlink on Windows needs SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege, which a test must not assume. This is the strongest evidence-path control in the repository -- a symlink planted inside the evidence root is the escape a path-string validator cannot catch -- so the gate does not pretend a Windows run covered it. It runs on Linux, which is the only platform the product installs on.

This is not a test; it is the child process of the kill -9 fault-injection drill at TestKilledMidStore, and it is a Test function only so it can reuse the test binary rather than being a second program. It is gated on an environment variable so an ordinary run does nothing. It appears in every run's skip list, which is noise with a name on it; renaming it would require a separate main package for no other gain, and this entry is what makes the noise accounted for.

Entirely mode assertions. Windows has a read-only flag and nothing else: os.Chmod cannot express 0640 and os.Stat reports a synthesised mode, so running this on Windows would be testing NTFS. Unlike the installer's equivalent, the whole test IS the mode assertion, so a conditional rather than a skip would be an empty test.

The same POSIX-modes condition as TestTheEnvironmentFileIsNotWorldReadable, on the re-install path: a preserved env file left world-readable by an older installer must be tightened, and the assertion is a permission bit. Windows cannot express one, so the control runs on Linux only.
